[[File:Laura Perin, Napoleone Ferrara, and Matteo Garbelotto.jpg|thumb|[[Laura Perin]], Napoleone Ferrara, and [[Matteo Garbelotto]]]]

'''Napoleone Ferrara''' (born 26 July 1956 in [[Catania]], Sicily, Italy) is an Italian-American molecular biologist who joined [[University of California, San Diego]] [[UC San Diego Health#Moores Cancer Center|Moores Cancer Center]] in 2013 after a career in Northern California at the biotechnology giant [[Genentech]], where he pioneered the development of new treatments for [[angiogenic]] diseases such as cancer, [[age-related macular degeneration|age-related macular degeneration (AMD)]], and [[diabetic retinopathy]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Napoleone Ferrara, MD:  Distinguished Professor of Pathology|url=https://healthsciences.ucsd.edu/research/moores/about/leadership/directors-office/Pages/basic-science.aspx|website=UC San Diego Health Sciences|access-date=8 June 2016}}</ref> At Genentech, he discovered [[Vascular endothelial growth factor|VEGF]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Leung |first=D. W. |last2=Cachianes |first2=G. |last3=Kuang |first3=W. J. |last4=Goeddel |first4=D. V. |last5=Ferrara |first5=N. |date=1989-12-08 |title=Vascular endothelial growth factor is a secreted angiogenic mitogen |url=https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2479986 |journal=Science  |volume=246 |issue=4935 |pages=1306–1309 |doi=10.1126/science.2479986 |issn=0036-8075 |pmid=2479986}}</ref>—and made the first anti-VEGF antibody—which suppresses growth of a variety of tumors.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kim |first=K. J. |last2=Li |first2=B. |last3=Winer |first3=J. |last4=Armanini |first4=M. |last5=Gillett |first5=N. |last6=Phillips |first6=H. S. |last7=Ferrara |first7=N. |date=1993-04-29 |title=Inhibition of vascular endothelial growth factor-induced angiogenesis suppresses tumour growth in vivo |url=https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7683111 |journal=Nature |volume=362 |issue=6423 |pages=841–844 |doi=10.1038/362841a0 |issn=0028-0836 |pmid=7683111}}</ref> These findings helped lead to development and FDA approval of the first clinically effective angiogenesis inhibitor, [[bevacizumab]] (Avastin), which prevents the growth of new blood vessels into a solid tumor. Bevacizumab, first approved for treatment of metastatic colorectal cancer in 2004,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hurwitz |first=Herbert |last2=Fehrenbacher |first2=Louis |last3=Novotny |first3=William |last4=Cartwright |first4=Thomas |last5=Hainsworth |first5=John |last6=Heim |first6=William |last7=Berlin |first7=Jordan |last8=Baron |first8=Ari |last9=Griffing |first9=Susan |last10=Holmgren |first10=Eric |last11=Ferrara |first11=Napoleone |last12=Fyfe |first12=Gwen |last13=Rogers |first13=Beth |last14=Ross |first14=Robert |last15=Kabbinavar |first15=Fairooz |date=2004-06-03 |title=Bevacizumab plus irinotecan, fluorouracil, and leucovorin for metastatic colorectal cancer |url=https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15175435 |journal=The New England Journal of Medicine |volume=350 |issue=23 |pages=2335–2342 |doi=10.1056/NEJMoa032691 |issn=1533-4406 |pmid=15175435}}</ref> has become part of standard treatment for a variety of cancers.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ferrara |first=Napoleone |last2=Adamis |first2=Anthony P. |date=June 2016 |title=Ten years of anti-vascular endothelial growth factor therapy |url=https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26775688 |journal=Nature Reviews. Drug Discovery |volume=15 |issue=6 |pages=385–403 |doi=10.1038/nrd.2015.17 |issn=1474-1784 |pmid=26775688}}</ref> Ferrara's work led also to the development of ranibizumab ([[Lucentis]]), a drug that is highly effective at preventing vision loss in patients with intraocular neovascular disorders such as neovascular AMD and retinal vein occlusion.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Cao |first=Yihai |last2=Langer |first2=Robert |last3=Ferrara |first3=Napoleone |date=June 2023 |title=Targeting angiogenesis in oncology, ophthalmology and beyond |url=https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37041221 |journal=Nature Reviews. Drug Discovery |volume=22 |issue=6 |pages=476–495 |doi=10.1038/s41573-023-00671-z |issn=1474-1784 |pmid=37041221}}</ref> Ranibizumab and other anti-VEGF agents represent the first effective therapy for such blinding disorders and rank among the most widely used drugs in older adults.

==Education and early career==
Ferrara received his medical degree from the [[University of Catania]], Italy, in 1981. He did post-doctoral research at the [[University of California, San Francisco]]. 

In 1988 he joined Genentech and worked there for about 25 years.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Knies-Bamforth |first1=Ulrike |last2=Watson |first2=Christopher |last3=Ferrara |first3=Napoleone |title=Napoleone Ferrara discusses Avastin™ and the future of anti-angiogenesis therapy |journal=Drug Discovery Today |date=April 2005 |volume=10 |issue=8 |pages=539–541 |doi=10.1016/S1359-6446(05)03411-2 |pmid=15837595 }}</ref>

==Current research==
Ferrara is Distinguished Professor of Pathology and Adjunct Professor of Ophthalmology at UC San Diego Health. He continues investigating  mechanisms of angiogenesis aiming to develop novel treatments  for cancer and ocular disorders.

==Selected honors and awards==
Ferrara is a member of both the US National Academy of Sciences and the US National Academy of Medicine.

Ferrara has received numerous awards. In 2005, he received the Grand Prix scientifique de la Fondation Lefoulon-Delalande, a major award in Cardiovascular Research.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://lefoulon-delalande.institut-de-france.fr/historique-0#12_le_grand_prix_scientifique_2005|title=Historique|date=2012-04-12|work=Fondation Lefoulon-Delalande Institut de France|access-date=2017-12-12}}</ref> In 2006, he was a recipient of the Passano Award and the General Motors Cancer Research Award. In 2010 he won the Lasker-deBakey Clinical Medical Research Award  for the VEGF discovery and the development of the first effective therapy for neovascular AMD.  In 2013, he was awarded the Breakthrough Prize in Life Sciences.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://breakthroughprizeinlifesciences.org/news1 |title=Breakthrough Prize in Life Sciences |access-date=25 September 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130926154106/http://breakthroughprizeinlifesciences.org/news1 |archive-date=26 September 2013 |url-status=dead }}</ref> In addition, he received the ASCO Science of Oncology Award (2007), the Pezcoller Foundation/AACR International Award (2009), the [[Dr. Paul Janssen Award for Biomedical Research]] (2011), and  [[the Economist]]'s [[The Economist innovation award|Innovation Award for Bioscience]] in 2012. In September 2014, Ferrara was awarded the António Champalimaud Vision Award from the [[Champalimaud Foundation]].<ref>''[http://health.ucsd.edu/news/releases/Pages/2014-09-10-ferrara-receives-champalimaud-prize.aspx Ferrara Receives Champalimaud Award for Role in Eye Disease Therapy]'', UC San Diego</ref> In the same year, he received the [[Canada Gairdner International Award]]. In 2023, he received the [[Keio Medical Science Prize]]<ref>[https://www.ms-fund.keio.ac.jp/prize/282023.html 第28回（2023年）受賞者]</ref> and the [[Prince Mahidol Award]] in Medicine.
